questions.q: What happens to the transaction log in SIMPLE recovery?
options: It is automatically truncated after every checkpoint once the transactions are no longer needed for crash recovery
It grows forever until manually truncated
It is never written to at all
It is truncated only when a log backup runs, same as FULL
questions.explain: SIMPLE recovery auto-truncates the log after checkpoint, which is why there's no log backup to take and no point-in-time recovery available.

questions.q: Which recovery model is required to support point-in-time recovery?
options: FULL (with a chain of full, differential, and log backups)
SIMPLE, because it truncates the log automatically
BULK_LOGGED, in every scenario without exception
None — point-in-time recovery isn't possible in SQL Server
questions.explain: FULL recovery retains every transaction in the log until a log backup runs, which is what allows restoring to a specific moment in time using full + log backups.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff of BULK_LOGGED recovery?
options: Bulk operations are minimally logged for speed, but you cannot point-in-time restore through a log backup window containing one
It behaves identically to SIMPLE in every respect
It disables the transaction log entirely
It permanently prevents differential backups
questions.explain: BULK_LOGGED minimally logs operations like BULK INSERT and SELECT INTO for performance, but a log backup spanning one of those operations can only be restored to its end, not to an arbitrary point inside it.

questions.q: How do you check a database's current recovery model?
options: Query recovery_model_desc from sys.databases
Run DBCC CHECKDB
Check the file extension of the .mdf file
Recovery model cannot be queried, only set
questions.explain: sys.databases exposes recovery_model_desc (SIMPLE, FULL, or BULK_LOGGED) for every database on the instance.

questions.q: After switching a database from SIMPLE to FULL recovery, when does point-in-time recovery actually become available?
options: Only after the next full backup starts a new log backup chain
Immediately, retroactive to when the database was created
Never — switching recovery models doesn't affect backup capability
Only after a server restart
questions.explain: The switch to FULL doesn't retroactively enable point-in-time recovery; the log backup chain only begins from the next full backup taken after the switch.
